L563: If full precision reductions are needed, users can disable reduced precision reductions in fp16 GEMMs with:
L564: 
L565:     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction = False
L566: Assigning a boolean is equivalent to assigning `(allow_reduced_precision, True)` and sets `allow_splitk` to `True`. To disable both reduced precision reductions and split-k reductions, assign `(allow_reduced_precision, allow_splitk)` explicitly:
L567: 
L568:     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction = (False, False)
L569: The current split-k setting can be queried with `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_reduced_precision_reduction_split_k`. The combination `(True, False)` is not supported because reduced precision reductions require split-k.
L570: 
L571: To toggle the reduced precision reduction flags in C++, one can do

L573:     at::globalContext().setAllowFP16ReductionCuBLAS(false, false);
L574: 
L575: 
L576: The second argument is `allow_splitk` and defaults to `true` when omitted.
L577: ## Reduced Precision Reduction in BF16 GEMMs【248†#】
L578: 
L579: A similar flag (as above) exists for BFloat16 GEMMs. Note that this switch is set to `True` by default for BF16, if you observe numerical instability in your workload, you may wish to set it to `False`.
L580: 
L581: If reduced precision reductions are not desired, users can disable reduced precision reductions in bf16 GEMMs with:
L582: 
L583:     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction = False
L584: Assigning a boolean is equivalent to assigning `(allow_reduced_precision, True)` and sets `allow_splitk` to `True`. To disable both reduced precision reductions and split-k reductions, assign `(allow_reduced_precision, allow_splitk)` explicitly:
L585: 
L586:     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction = (False, False)
L587: The current split-K setting can be queried with `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction_split_k`. The combination `(True, False)` is not supported because reduced precision reductions require split-K.
L588: 
L589: To toggle the reduced precision reduction flags in C++, one can do
L590: 
L591:     at::globalContext().setAllowBF16ReductionCuBLAS(false, false);
L592: 
L593: 
L594: The second argument is `allow_splitk` and defaults to `true` when omitted.
L595: ## Full FP16 Accumulation in FP16 GEMMs【249†#】
L596: 
L597: Certain GPUs have increased performance when doing all FP16 GEMM accumulation in FP16, at the cost of numerical precision and greater likelihood of overflow. Note that this setting only has an effect on GPUs of compute capability 7.0 (Volta) or newer.
L598: 
L599: This behavior can be enabled via:
L600: 
L601:     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_fp16_accumulation = True
L602: To toggle the reduced precision reduction flags in C++, one can do
L603: 
L604:     at::globalContext().setAllowFP16AccumulationCuBLAS(true);
L605: ## Asynchronous execution【250†#】
L606: 
L607: By default, GPU operations are asynchronous. When you call a function that uses the GPU, the operations are enqueued to the particular device, but not necessarily executed until later. This allows us to execute more computations in parallel, including operations on CPU or other GPUs.
L608: In general, the effect of asynchronous computation is invisible to the caller, because (1) each device executes operations in the order they are queued, and (2) PyTorch automatically performs necessary synchronization when copying data between CPU and GPU or between two GPUs. Hence, computation will proceed as if every operation was executed synchronously.
L609: You can force synchronous computation by setting environment variable `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. This can be handy when an error occurs on the GPU. (With asynchronous execution, such an error isn’t reported until after the operation is actually executed, so the stack trace does not show where it was requested.)
L610: A consequence of the asynchronous computation is that time measurements without synchronizations are not accurate. To get precise measurements, one should either call 【251†`torch.cuda.synchronize()`】 before measuring, or use 【252†`torch.cuda.Event`】 to record times as following:
L611: 
L612:     start_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
L613:     end_event = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
L614:     start_event.record()
L615: 
L616:     # Run some things here
L617: 
L618:     end_event.record()
L619:     torch.cuda.synchronize()  # Wait for the events to be recorded!
L620:     elapsed_time_ms = start_event.elapsed_time(end_event)
L621: As an exception, several functions such as 【239†`to()`】 and 【238†`copy_()`】 admit an explicit `non_blocking` argument, which lets the caller bypass synchronization when it is unnecessary. Another exception is CUDA streams, explained below.
L622: ### CUDA streams【253†#】
L623: 
L624: A 【254†CUDA stream†docs.nvidia.com】 is a linear sequence of execution that belongs to a specific device. You normally do not need to create one explicitly: by default, each device uses its own “default” stream.
L625: Operations inside each stream are serialized in the order they are created, but operations from different streams can execute concurrently in any relative order, unless explicit synchronization functions (such as 【251†`synchronize()`】 or 【255†`wait_stream()`】) are used. For example, the following code is incorrect:
L626: 
L627:     cuda = torch.device('cuda')
L628:     s = torch.cuda.Stream()  # Create a new stream.
L629:     A = torch.empty((100, 100), device=cuda).normal_(0.0, 1.0)
L630:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L631:         # sum() may start execution before normal_() finishes!
L632:         B = torch.sum(A)
L633: When the “current stream” is the default stream, PyTorch automatically performs necessary synchronization when data is moved around, as explained above. However, when using non-default streams, it is the user’s responsibility to ensure proper synchronization. The fixed version of this example is:
L634: 
L635:     cuda = torch.device('cuda')
L636:     s = torch.cuda.Stream()  # Create a new stream.
L637:     A = torch.empty((100, 100), device=cuda).normal_(0.0, 1.0)
L638:     s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.default_stream(cuda))  # NEW!
L639:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L640:         B = torch.sum(A)
L641:     A.record_stream(s)  # NEW!
L642: There are two new additions. The 【255†`torch.cuda.Stream.wait_stream()`】 call ensures that the `normal_()` execution has finished before we start running `sum(A)` on a side stream. The 【256†`torch.Tensor.record_stream()`】 (see for more details) ensures that we do not deallocate A before `sum(A)` has completed.
L643: You can also manually wait on the stream at some later point in time with `torch.cuda.default_stream(cuda).wait_stream(s)` (note that it is pointless to wait immediately, since that will prevent the stream execution from running in parallel with other work on the default stream.) See the documentation for 【256†`torch.Tensor.record_stream()`】 on more details on when to use one or another.
L644: Note that this synchronization is necessary even when there is no read dependency, e.g., as seen in this example:
L645: 
L646:     cuda = torch.device('cuda')
L647:     s = torch.cuda.Stream()  # Create a new stream.
L648:     A = torch.empty((100, 100), device=cuda)
L649:     s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.default_stream(cuda))  # STILL REQUIRED!
L650:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L651:         A.normal_(0.0, 1.0)
L652:         A.record_stream(s)
L653: Despite the computation on `s` not reading the contents of `A` and no other uses of `A`, it is still necessary to synchronize, because `A` may correspond to memory reallocated by the CUDA caching allocator, with pending operations from the old (deallocated) memory.
L654: ### Stream semantics of backward passes【257†#】
L655: 
L656: Each backward CUDA op runs on the same stream that was used for its corresponding forward op. If your forward pass runs independent ops in parallel on different streams, this helps the backward pass exploit that same parallelism.
L657: The stream semantics of a backward call with respect to surrounding ops are the same as for any other call. The backward pass inserts internal syncs to ensure this even when backward ops run on multiple streams as described in the previous paragraph.
L658: More concretely, when calling 【258†`autograd.backward`】, 【259†`autograd.grad`】, or 【260†`tensor.backward`】, and optionally supplying CUDA tensor(s) as the initial gradient(s) (e.g., 【258†`autograd.backward(..., grad_tensors=initial_grads)`】, 【259†`autograd.grad(..., grad_outputs=initial_grads)`】, or 【260†`tensor.backward(..., gradient=initial_grad)`】), the acts of
L659:   1. optionally populating initial gradient(s),
L660: 
L661:   2. invoking the backward pass, and
L662: 
L663:   3. using the gradients
L664: have the same stream-semantics relationship as any group of ops:
L665: 
L666:     s = torch.cuda.Stream()
L667: 
L668:     # Safe, grads are used in the same stream context as backward()
L669:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L670:         loss.backward()
L671:         use grads
L672: 
L673:     # Unsafe
L674:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L675:         loss.backward()
L676:     use grads
L677: 
L678:     # Safe, with synchronization
L679:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L680:         loss.backward()
L681:     torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)
L682:     use grads
L683:     # Safe, populating initial grad and invoking backward are in the same stream context
L684:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L685:         loss.backward(gradient=torch.ones_like(loss))
L686: 
L687:     # Unsafe, populating initial_grad and invoking backward are in different stream contexts,
L688:     # without synchronization
L689:     initial_grad = torch.ones_like(loss)
L690:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L691:         loss.backward(gradient=initial_grad)
L692: 
L693:     # Safe, with synchronization
L694:     initial_grad = torch.ones_like(loss)
L695:     s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
L696:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L697:         initial_grad.record_stream(s)
L698:         loss.backward(gradient=initial_grad)
L699: #### BC note: Using grads on the default stream【261†#】
L700: 
L701: In prior versions of PyTorch (1.9 and earlier), the autograd engine always synced the default stream with all backward ops, so the following pattern:
L702: 
L703:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L704:         loss.backward()
L705:     use grads
L706: was safe as long as `use grads` happened on the default stream. In present PyTorch, that pattern is no longer safe. If `backward()` and `use grads` are in different stream contexts, you must sync the streams:
L707: 
L708:     with torch.cuda.stream(s):
L709:         loss.backward()
L710:     torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s)
L711:     use grads
L712: 
L713: 
L714: even if `use grads` is on the default stream.
L715: ## Memory management【262†#】
L716: PyTorch uses a caching memory allocator to speed up memory allocations. This allows fast memory deallocation without device synchronizations. However, the unused memory managed by the allocator will still show as if used in `nvidia-smi`. You can use `memory_allocated()` and `max_memory_allocated()` to monitor memory occupied by tensors, and use `memory_reserved()` and `max_memory_reserved()` to monitor the total amount of memory managed by the caching allocator.
L717: Calling `empty_cache()` releases all unused cached memory from PyTorch so that those can be used by other GPU applications. However, the occupied GPU memory by tensors will not be freed so it can not increase the amount of GPU memory available for PyTorch.
L718: To better understand how CUDA memory is being used over time, 【263†Understanding CUDA Memory Usage】 describes tools for capturing and visualizing traces of memory use.
L719: 
L720: For more advanced users, we offer more comprehensive memory benchmarking via `memory_stats()`. We also offer the capability to capture a complete snapshot of the memory allocator state via `memory_snapshot()`, which can help you understand the underlying allocation patterns produced by your code.
L721: ### Optimizing memory usage with `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF`【264†#】
L722: 
L723: Use of a caching allocator can interfere with memory checking tools such as `cuda-memcheck`. To debug memory errors using `cuda-memcheck`, set `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1` in your environment to disable caching.
L724: The behavior of the caching allocator can be controlled via the environment variable `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF`. `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF` is its alias and is provided only for backward compatibility. The format is `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=<option>:<value>,<option2>:<value2>...` Available options:
L725:   * `backend` allows selecting the underlying allocator implementation. Currently, valid options are `native`, which uses PyTorch’s native implementation, and `cudaMallocAsync`, which uses 【265†CUDA’s built-in asynchronous allocator†developer.nvidia.com】. `cudaMallocAsync` requires CUDA 11.4 or newer. The default is `native`. `backend` applies to all devices used by the process, and can’t be specified on a per-device basis.
L726:   * `large_segment_size_mb` the native allocator uses small and large blocks to manage allocated memory. This setting is used to configure the size of the large block. The default value is 20 MB.
L727:   * `max_split_size_mb` prevents the native allocator from splitting blocks larger than this size (in MB). This can reduce fragmentation and may allow some borderline workloads to complete without running out of memory. Performance cost can range from ‘zero’ to ‘substantial’ depending on allocation patterns. Default value is unlimited, i.e. all blocks can be split. The `memory_stats()` and `memory_summary()` methods are useful for tuning.
L728: This option should be used as a last resort for a workload that is aborting due to ‘out of memory’ and showing a large amount of inactive split blocks. `max_split_size_mb` is only meaningful with `backend:native`. With `backend:cudaMallocAsync`, `max_split_size_mb` is ignored.
